# An In-Depth Review of *Middlemarch* by George Eliot

## "The History of Man's Condition Has Not Yet Been Written": A Comprehensive Study of George Eliot's Masterwork

---

## Preface: Why *Middlemarch* Demands Our Attention

There is a particular kind of novel that does not merely tell a story but constructs a world so complete, so morally and psychologically intricate, that the reader emerges from it changed — not in the dramatic, sudden way of a revelation, but in the slow, accumulating way of genuine experience. George Eliot's *Middlemarch: A Study of Provincial Life*, published in installments between 1871 and 1872, is precisely such a novel. Virginia Woolf called it "one of the few English novels written for grown-up people." Henry James, who was not given to easy praise, described it as "a treasure-house of detail, but... an indifferent whole" — a judgment that, while famously wrong about the whole, at least acknowledges the extraordinary richness of the parts. Martin Amis placed it at the top of his list of the greatest novels in the English language. Zadie Smith has written about it with the reverence usually reserved for sacred texts.

What is it about this long, dense, Victorian novel — set in a fictional English Midlands town during the years 1829–1832, concerned with the Reform Bill, medical politics, marriage, inheritance, and the quiet disasters of ordinary ambition — that continues to compel readers nearly a century and a half after its publication? Why does a book about people who are, by any conventional measure, failures — a woman who wanted to be a saint and became a housewife, a doctor who wanted to revolutionize medicine and became a provincial practitioner — feel not like a tragedy but like one of the most life-affirming works in the English language?

This review attempts to answer those questions by examining *Middlemarch* in depth: its narrative architecture, its major themes, its stylistic innovations, its characters, its historical context, and its enduring relevance. I will argue that *Middlemarch* is not merely a great Victorian novel but one of the supreme achievements of the novel as a form — a work that takes the full measure of human limitation and, in doing so, paradoxically expands our sense of what human life can mean.

---

## Part One: The Author and Her World

### George Eliot: The Woman Behind the Pseudonym

To understand *Middlemarch*, one must first understand something of the extraordinary woman who wrote it. Mary Ann Evans (1819–1880) adopted the pen name George Eliot for reasons both practical and philosophical. In the Victorian literary marketplace, women writers were often dismissed or condescended to; a male name would ensure that her work was taken seriously on its own terms before readers knew its author's sex. But the pseudonym also represented something deeper: a kind of self-creation, a deliberate construction of an authorial identity that could speak with authority on subjects — philosophy, science, politics, theology — that Victorian society considered beyond the proper sphere of women.

Evans was, by any measure, one of the most intellectually formidable people of her age. She taught herself German, Italian, Greek, Latin, and Hebrew. She translated Strauss's *Das Leben Jesu* (1846) and Feuerbach's *Das Wesen des Christenthums* (1854) — works of radical biblical criticism that contributed to her loss of Christian faith. She served as the de facto editor of the *Westminster Review*, one of the leading intellectual journals of the day, where she published essays on philosophy, literature, and science. She was intimate with Herbert Spencer, John Stuart Mill, Thomas Carlyle, and Charles Darwin. She lived, from 1854 until his death in 1878, with the philosopher and critic George Henry Lewes in a relationship that, because Lewes was legally unable to divorce his estranged wife, could not be formalized as marriage — a fact that made her a social outcast in respectable Victorian society, even as her novels made her the most celebrated writer in England.

This biography matters for *Middlemarch* in several ways. Eliot's intellectual range — her command of philosophy, science, theology, history, and economics — gives the novel its extraordinary density of reference and its capacity to situate individual lives within the largest possible frameworks of meaning. Her experience of social ostracism gives her a particular sensitivity to the ways in which society constrains and punishes those who deviate from its norms, especially women. Her loss of religious faith, combined with her retention of a deeply ethical sensibility, shapes the novel's moral vision: a humanism that takes seriously the need for meaning and connection in a world that can no longer guarantee them through supernatural sanction.

### The Historical Moment: Reform, Science, and the Crisis of Belief

*Middlemarch* is set in the years 1829–1832, a period of intense political and social ferment in England. The Reform Act of 1832, which extended the franchise and redistributed parliamentary seats, was the great political event of the era — a moment when the old order of aristocratic privilege was beginning, slowly and painfully, to give way to something more democratic. The novel's characters are acutely aware of this political context: Will Ladislaw works as a journalist and political agitator for reform; the question of who will represent Middlemarch in Parliament is a matter of intense local concern; the old Tory landowners like Brooke and Chettam are being forced to reckon with new political realities.

But the novel is set in 1829–1832 and written in 1869–1872 — a gap of roughly forty years that is itself significant. Eliot is writing about the past from the vantage point of a present that knows how that past turned out. The Reform Act passed, but it did not transform England into a democracy overnight; the process of reform was slow, contested, and incomplete. By writing about this earlier moment of political hope and disappointment, Eliot is implicitly commenting on the political situation of her own time — the Second Reform Act of 1867 had just extended the franchise further, but the question of what genuine social transformation would require remained open.

The period was also one of scientific revolution. The 1830s saw the beginnings of the geological and biological discoveries that would culminate in Darwin's *On the Origin of Species* (1859). Lydgate's medical research — his interest in the "primitive tissue" that underlies all organic life — reflects the scientific spirit of the age, the conviction that patient empirical investigation could unlock the secrets of nature. Eliot herself was deeply engaged with the science of her time; she had read Darwin carefully and was friends with Herbert Spencer, whose evolutionary philosophy she found both compelling and troubling.

And the period was one of religious crisis. The Higher Criticism of the Bible, which Eliot had helped to introduce to English readers through her translations, was undermining the historical foundations of Christian belief. The Oxford Movement was attempting to revitalize the Church of England through a return to Catholic tradition. Evangelicalism was transforming the religious landscape of provincial England. Dorothea Brooke's intense religiosity, her desire for a life of saintly dedication, is set against this background of religious ferment — a background in which the old certainties are dissolving and new forms of meaning are urgently needed.

---

## Part Two: The Architecture of the Novel

### Structure and Form

*Middlemarch* is a long novel — roughly 900 pages in most modern editions — and its length is not incidental to its meaning. Eliot needs space to do what she wants to do: to show how lives unfold over time, how character is revealed through accumulated small choices rather than single dramatic decisions, how the social web of a community shapes and constrains individual possibility. The novel's length is an argument about the nature of human experience: that it is dense, interconnected, and resistant to the simplifications of plot.

The novel was originally published in eight "books," each with its own title: "Miss Brooke," "Old and Young," "Waiting for Death," "Three Love Problems," "The Dead Hand," "The Widow and the Wife," "Two Temptations," and "Sunset and Sunrise." These titles are themselves significant: they suggest the novel's concern with time (waiting, sunset, sunrise), with social relationships (widow, wife, love problems), and with the moral drama of individual choice (temptations, the dead hand of the past). The book structure also reflects the novel's serial publication history; each installment was designed to be satisfying in itself while also advancing the larger narrative.

The novel interweaves four main narrative strands: the story of Dorothea Brooke and her disastrous first marriage to the scholar Edward Casaubon, followed by her love for Will Ladislaw; the story of Tertius Lydgate, the ambitious young doctor, and his marriage to the beautiful, shallow Rosamond Vincy; the story of Fred Vincy and Mary Garth, a more conventional love story that nonetheless carries significant thematic weight; and the story of Nicholas Bulstrode, the pious banker whose hidden past eventually destroys him. These strands are interwoven with extraordinary skill: characters from one strand appear in others, events in one plot have consequences in another, and the whole is held together by the social fabric of Middlemarch itself.

This multi-plot structure is one of the novel's great formal achievements. It allows Eliot to explore the same themes — the relationship between idealism and reality, the constraints of social convention, the nature of marriage, the possibility of moral growth — from multiple angles simultaneously. Dorothea and Lydgate are parallel figures: both are idealists who make disastrous marriages, both are constrained by the social expectations of their gender, both are ultimately defeated by the world's resistance to their ambitions. But they are also contrasting figures: Dorothea's idealism is moral and spiritual, Lydgate's is intellectual and professional; Dorothea's defeat is softened by her eventual happiness with Ladislaw, while Lydgate's is more complete and more bitter.

### The Narrator's Voice

One of the most distinctive features of *Middlemarch* is its narrator — a presence so powerful, so intellectually commanding, so morally serious, that she (and the narrator is implicitly gendered female, though this is never stated explicitly) becomes almost a character in her own right. The narrator of *Middlemarch* is not a neutral, invisible presence; she is constantly intervening in the narrative, commenting on characters and events, drawing philosophical conclusions, making connections between the particular and the general.

This narratorial voice is one of the great achievements of Victorian fiction. It combines intellectual authority with emotional warmth, philosophical depth with practical wisdom, irony with sympathy. Consider the famous opening of the Prelude:

> "Who that cares much to know the history of man, and how the mysterious mixture behaves under the varying experiments of Time, has not dwelt, at least briefly, on the life of Saint Theresa, has not smiled with some gentleness at the thought of the little girl walking forth one morning hand-in-hand with her still smaller brother, to go and seek martyrdom in the country of the Moors?"

This opening immediately establishes the narrator's characteristic mode: the appeal to a community of thoughtful readers ("who that cares much to know"), the historical and philosophical sweep (Saint Theresa, the history of man), the combination of grandeur and intimacy (the little girl walking hand-in-hand with her brother). The narrator is positioning herself — and us — as people who take seriously the question of how human beings live and what their lives mean.

The narrator's irony is equally characteristic. When she describes Casaubon's courtship of Dorothea, she writes:

> "He had not had much foretaste of happiness in his previous life. To know intense joy without a strong bodily frame, one must have an enthusiastic soul. Mr. Casaubon had never had a strong bodily frame, and his soul was sensitive without being enthusiastic: it was too languid to thrill out of self-consciousness into passionate delight; it went on fluttering in the swampy ground where it was hatched, thinking of its wings and never flying."

This is devastating — the image of the soul "fluttering in the swampy ground where it was hatched, thinking of its wings and never flying" is one of the most precise and cruel characterizations in English fiction. But the narrator immediately follows this with something more sympathetic:

> "His experience was of that pitiable kind which shrinks from pity, and fears most of all that it should be known: it was that proud narrow sensitiveness which has not mass enough to spare for transformation into sympathy, and quivers thread-like in small currents of self-preoccupation or at best of an egoism which mistakes itself for exquisite susceptibility."

The narrator understands Casaubon's limitations with a clarity that is almost clinical, but she also understands the suffering that underlies them. This combination of clear-eyed judgment and genuine compassion is the hallmark of Eliot's moral vision.

The narrator also frequently steps back from the immediate narrative to offer what we might call philosophical interludes — passages of extended reflection on the nature of human experience that go beyond what any individual character could articulate. The most famous of these is the "pier-glass" passage in Chapter 27:

> "An eminent philosopher among my friends, who can dignify even your ugly furniture by lifting it into the serene light of science, has shown me this pregnant little fact. Your pier-glass or extensive surface of polished steel made to be rubbed by a housemaid, will be minutely and multitudinously scratched in all directions; but place now against it a lighted candle as a centre of illumination, and lo! the scratches will seem to arrange themselves in a fine series of concentric circles round that little sun. It is demonstrable that the scratches are going everywhere impartially, and it is only your candle which produces the flattering illusion of a concentric arrangement, its light falling with an exclusive optical selection. These things are a parable. The scratches are events, and the candle is the egoism of any person now absent — of Miss Vincy, for example."

This passage is doing several things at once. It is making a philosophical point about the nature of egoism — the way in which the self naturally arranges the world around itself as a center. It is making a methodological point about the novel itself — that Eliot's narrative technique involves illuminating the same events from multiple perspectives, showing how each character's "candle" of self-interest creates a different pattern. And it is making a moral point — that the recognition of our own egoism is the beginning of genuine sympathy and moral growth.

---

## Part Three: The Major Characters

### Dorothea Brooke: The Saint Without a Cause

Dorothea Brooke is one of the great characters of English fiction — not because she is admirable in a simple, uncomplicated way, but because she is so fully realized in her contradictions. She is idealistic, generous, passionate, and intelligent; she is also naive, self-deceiving, and capable of a kind of spiritual arrogance that is all the more dangerous for being unconscious.

The novel opens with a description of Dorothea that immediately establishes her complexity:

> "Miss Brooke had that kind of beauty which seems to be thrown into relief by poor dress. Her hand and wrist were so finely formed that she could wear sleeves not less bare of style than those in which the Blessed Virgin appeared to Italian painters; and her profile as well as her stature and bearing seemed to gain the more dignity from her plain garments, which by the side of provincial fashion gave her the impressiveness of a fine quotation from the Bible, — or from one of our elder poets, — in a paragraph of to-day's newspaper."

This description is doing something subtle and important. Dorothea is beautiful, but her beauty is of a particular kind — it is enhanced by plainness, by the absence of ornament. She is compared to the Blessed Virgin, to the Bible, to "our elder poets" — she is, from the beginning, associated with a kind of spiritual grandeur that is at odds with the "paragraph of to-day's newspaper," with the ordinary, provincial world she inhabits. The comparison is both admiring and slightly ironic: Dorothea's spiritual aspirations are genuine, but they are also somewhat out of place in the world she actually lives in.

Dorothea's first great mistake is her marriage to Edward Casaubon. She convinces herself that Casaubon is a great scholar, a man of vast intellectual and spiritual resources, and that by marrying him she will be able to participate in his great work — the "Key to All Mythologies" — and thereby achieve the kind of meaningful, dedicated life she craves. The narrator is clear about the self-deception involved:

> "She had not reached that point of renunciation at which she would have been satisfied with having a wise husband: she wished, poor child, to be wise herself. Miss Brooke had a naive delight in the fact that she had chosen to marry a man who was so much older than herself, and who had so much more knowledge than she had. She was not in the least aware that she was choosing a man who would be a disappointment to her."

The marriage to Casaubon is one of the great disasters in Victorian fiction, and Eliot renders it with extraordinary psychological precision. The honeymoon in Rome — where Dorothea, surrounded by the overwhelming weight of classical civilization, begins to realize the emptiness of her husband's scholarship and the coldness of his heart — is one of the most powerful sequences in the novel. The image of Dorothea weeping in her Roman apartment, surrounded by the ruins of a civilization she cannot access, is both literally and symbolically resonant: she is imprisoned by the past, by the dead weight of Casaubon's scholarship, by the social conventions that have made her a wife rather than an independent agent.
